label: Claude Fable 5.2
output:
**Last night**

I did my last ever night shift on Saturday. 7 November, 21:00 to 07:30, majors. As of Monday I'm on the days-only rota, and I've been trying to write about it ever since. Every attempt has turned into either a eulogy or a complaint about the NHS. Nobody has died and I've written enough complaints on here already, so this is going to try to be neither. (Also, hello. I know it's been since spring.)

Some facts first. My first night shift was in 2012, as an SHO. That makes fourteen years. I'm 42, my knees have views, and my sleep hasn't been right for a long time. My GP told me recently that my blood pressure is not a joke anymore, which stung, because I had been treating it as one. So I'm moving to days, and I'm relieved.

I also feel like a traitor for being relieved. I might as well say that now, since it's the thing every other draft was written around.

I want to be honest about what nights took, so I'll start there.

My first winter of nights, I sat in the car park at the Infirmary after a shift and cried because I couldn't remember whether I'd given the second dose. I had. But I didn't know that for the length of time I sat there, and I can still see the frost on the windscreen, the exact pattern of it. I've forgotten whole years of my thirties and I remember that frost.

My sister lives in Bangalore. I missed both my nieces' naming ceremonies. I was only ever going to be there on video, which is a poor enough substitute, and both times I was on nights and didn't even manage that. She has never once complained about it. She reads this blog, so: I noticed. I always noticed.

And then the ordinary losses, which add up. Years of sleeping through daylight. Being the person who can't come. Eating dinner at breakfast time and not really knowing what day it is by the third one in a row. The knees.

Now what nights gave me, which is harder to write about without getting soft.

Nights are where the department is most itself. There are fewer managers about and, I think as a direct result, more honesty. People say what they mean at 3am. There's also more kindness, which I can't fully explain. Perhaps it's that there are fewer of you and nobody is coming, so you look after each other because who else will.

People think nights are about adrenaline. There is some of that. But mostly it's about staying kind at 5am when you are empty. That's the whole skill, as far as I can tell. The medicine you can learn from books. Being decent to a frightened person when you have nothing left and two and a half hours to go, that you only learn by doing it badly a few times and resolving to do it better.

Last winter, at about three in the morning, an old gentleman held my hand and told me I had his daughter's hands. That's all I'm going to say about him, except that he went home three days later. I've had a lot of things said to me on nights. That one I've kept.

Then there's Folasade, our charge nurse on nights, who has been doing this for 22 years. That's eight more than me, and she still beats me up the stairs. I don't mean that as a figure of speech. I mean we have taken the same stairs at the same time and she has got to the top first, repeatedly, and not been out of breath when I arrived. I've learned more from watching her talk to relatives than from most courses I've been sent on.

And there's the toast. At 4am, someone makes toast in the staff room. This has been true for as long as I've worked there. Nobody admits to starting it. You never see the first slice go in. You just become aware, around four, that there is toast, and a small crowd, and for about ten minutes everyone is slightly more human. I have asked. I've been asking for years. Everyone says they thought it was someone else.

On Sunday morning I drove home down the London Road with the sun coming up and the shipping forecast on catch-up, which is how I've ended more night shifts than I could count. Somewhere along there I realised I wouldn't see that light from this side again. I'll see plenty of sunrises. I'll be driving into work under them like a normal person. But there's a particular way the morning looks when you've been up all night and everyone you were responsible for is still there, handed over, somebody else's now. I'll see the same light on the way in, but it won't look like that.

I didn't cry, for the record. Fourteen years on from the car park, I'd call that progress, or possibly just tiredness.

So I'm relieved, and I feel like a traitor, and I think both of those are allowed to be true for a while. My blood pressure will presumably be pleased. I'll get to be awake at the same time as the people I love, including two nieces who are owed a great many video calls.

But I don't want to end on me. It carries on without me, and that's how it should be. Tonight at nine a team will take handover in majors, and Folasade will very likely be among them, and she will get up the stairs before whoever has replaced me. And at four o'clock tomorrow morning, somebody will make toast.

If you're on tonight and it's you who starts it, you can tell me. I'm off the rota now. I won't say a word.

---

That comes to roughly 950 words, so there's room to add. Three things to check:

- **The patient:** I kept him to exactly what you gave me. If "last winter" plus "three days later" still feels too specific for colleagues reading, change it to "a while ago" and "a few days later".
- **Folasade:** she's named with her role and years of service, so make sure she's happy with that before you post.
- **The ending:** the line saying she'll very likely be on tonight is my guess. Adjust it if you know her rota.
